CDIAL 8416 paútra explicitly records Shina pōc̣ṷ grandson; its full entry and addendum contain no separate Shina subsection or borrowing qualification. Degener independently gives póoc̣o Enkel with T. 8416. The Schmidt, Rajapurohit and HKAT forms preserve the same long-vowel and affricate stem. HKAT uses it for both son’s son and daughter’s son, an extension of the narrower Old Indo-Aryan relationship.

The Rajapurohit granddaughter form pā́ʦ̣i is compared with the explicitly cited Shina pōc̣i̯ under CDIAL 8417 pautrī and Degener póoc̣i. Its ā rather than ō remains unexplained by these entries; the feminine ending, affricate and kinship meaning support the family comparison, but this attestation needs vowel/transcription review.

CDIAL 8693 prapautra explicitly includes Lorimer’s Shina paōčo great-grandson and feminine paōči, while marking the affricate interpretation uncertain (= c̣?). Rajapurohit’s pahṓʦ̣o and pahṓʦ̣i have the matching great-grandchild semantics and gender contrast. The medial h is not explained by the cited entry and the affricate notation needs review, so the proposed family link remains difficult rather than a settled sound correspondence.

CDIAL 12753 śváśura explicitly gives Shina Gilgit šaiŭr, Gurezi šāir and Palesi šēr father-in-law. The long-vowel and diphthongal modern forms match this attested dialect range; HKAT’s final vowel is retained. The source includes both wife’s and husband’s father within the inherited meaning, and its borrowing comments concern other languages, not these Shina forms.

CDIAL 12759 śvaśrū explicitly records Shina šăṣ mother-in-law. The modern śaṣ/śáṣ forms preserve the contrasting initial and final sibilants, and both wife’s mother and husband’s mother fall within the head’s meaning. Degener independently cites T. 12759 for šyaṣ Schwiegermutter. No separate subsection or Shina donor qualification intervenes.

The relevant branch of CDIAL 5198 is subsection 2 *jāmātra-/°aka-, which explicitly lists Shina žămc̣ō and dialect variants including Gurezi žamac̣ōh. The outward arrow to Domaaki does not make Shina a borrowing. Rajapurohit and HKAT have compatible son-in-law forms with the medial affricate; Degener also cites T. 5198 for ǰamac̣oó. The variation in initial sibilant/affricate and medial vowel is preserved.

CDIAL 9089 groups *phupphu-, *phupphī- and *phapphī- in one head and explicitly gives Shina phīpī/phīpi for father’s sister and mother’s brother’s wife. The modern phīpi and phapī series share this expressive kinship family. Rajapurohit’s final h, HKAT’s masculine-final phipō for uncle’s wife, and variable aspiration are retained as review points; the proposal does not pretend to select one uniquely recoverable proto-vowel from the grouped head. Rajapurohit also separately records phapī and phapyē for maternal uncle’s wife, the second relationship explicitly included in Turner’s Shina gloss; the latter ending is retained as an inflectional review point.

CDIAL 8283 purāṇa explicitly gives Shina Gilgit purōnu, Gurezi prōṇu and Kohistani pōṇu old. Rajapurohit prṓno fits the contracted prōn- family, with dental rather than retroflex nasal in the transcription retained. The addendum does not impose a borrowing qualification on Shina.

CDIAL 12774 śveta explicitly cites Shina šeo, šyō and šīu white, as well as Jijal šɔ in silver. Rajapurohit śō is a contracted member of this documented white-adjective series; the absence of an overt glide is retained as a dialect review point. It is kept separate from the similarly shaped good adjective under śubha.

CDIAL 10896 laghu includes Shina lōku light, quick, active in its -kk- extension paragraph. Rajapurohit lóko light agrees with that explicitly cited Shina form. The extension has no separate numbered parent record; the proposal points to the head while preserving the relevant morphological paragraph. Same-page and numbered addenda do not alter this Shina comparison. CDIAL 10896 places this velar-extended form under the -kk- extension paragraph (*laghukk-, 10896-5), not the bare head; re-homed 2026-09-18.

CDIAL 10978 lavaṇa explicitly lists Shina Kohistani luṇi, Gurezi lūṇi and Jijal lūṇi salt, matching the long-vowel feminine forms in Schmidt and Rajapurohit. The entry questions the remote history of lavaṇa itself, preferring a Middle Indo-Aryan formation related to cutting or a piece of rock salt; this uncertainty is preserved, while the immediate Shina family comparison is explicit.

Schmidt iś and Rajapurohit iṣ bear are provisionally compared with the Shina affricate forms explicitly listed under CDIAL 2445 ṛkṣa. Neighboring Torwali īṣ and Phalura ĩṣ demonstrate fricative outcomes in the wider family, but do not establish either a Shina sound change or an immediate donor. The discrepant fricative place and loss of affrication remain source and dialect checks, so these records are difficult.
